gap: The caret is quantized hard to the pixel grid — every pixel x=357-362, y=93-166 is exactly #00BFFF with no fractional coverage anywhere — so it cannot land on the true sub-pixel text metric between characters (up to ~0.5px position error) and any motion between positions must step in whole pixels rather than glide. Combined with wholly square butt ends on a 6px width, it reads as a machined slab, closer to a one-character block selection than to a nib.
gapTheirs: The caret is subpixel-smeared and round-capped instead of hard-edged: it spreads over 7 columns (x=357-363) but only 5 of them are full #00BFFF, with the left edge at ~80% coverage (#31CAFE) and the right at ~20% (#C7ECF8); the tips fade to #66D6FC over a ~2px corner radius, so the top two rows are 4px and 6px wide against a 7px middle. Net: a 6px stroke delivered as a soft blue lozenge with no crisp edge on any of its four sides, versus B's 6x74 of pure #00BFFF with zero antialiased pixels.
verdict: These are the same caret rendered two ways, and A blinks its own edges away: at 6px wide, losing 20-80% of the coverage on the outer columns and rounding the tips turns the insertion point into a fat blue pill you have to squint at to place between the 'l' and the 'a'. B's is a hard bar you can aim with. Neither earns much credit — both fill 74px, the entire line pitch, 1.8x the 41px ascender-to-descender span, and both are ~1.5x the 4px stem weight of the body, so in either app the caret is fatter than the letters it stands between and butts straight into the following 'a' with zero clearance. B wins on the only axis that separates them: it is actually sharp.

states.name: selection
states.gap: A's band is the heavier of the two by 4px — 74px tall over a 41px ink extent (1.8x), tinting 18px of leading above the cap and 15px of empty leading below the descender, so in the single-line state actually shown it reads as a slab of tint rather than a marked phrase; B's bottom edge sits 2px closer to the type.
states.gapTheirs: B's band is 70px against a 74px line pitch — 94.6% — so it cannot tile: any selection crossing a line break leaves a 4px stripe of #F7F7F7 paper between every pair of rows, and the band is 18px above the cap vs 13px below the descender (5px asymmetric, riding ~2.5px high on the glyphs) where A's 18/15 is nearly centred.
states.verdict: A piece named 'Cursor & caret' and neither frame contains a caret — no bar, no accent pixel, no ink column anywhere in 800x260. That is the real failure here and both own it equally, so this comes down to 4px of selection band, which is a thin thing to decide a caret on. A wins because 74px is exactly the line pitch and B's 70px is not: drag over a paragraph in B and the highlight breaks into venetian blinds, which every writer has seen and no writer wants. Neither image gives me anything to say about caret width, height ratio, blink, or how it sits against a glyph edge, because neither shows one.
secondary: No caret in either image: scanned all 800 columns for isolated vertical dark runs and for any saturated pixel; nothing but glyph stems and the selection fill.
Selection fill identical: #CCEDF8 in both, hard 1px boundary, zero antialiasing on the band edge.
Anchor identical in both: band left edge x=220, 1-2px inside the 'T' stem; both bands start at y=95.
B carries a global ±1 RGB dither (34KB PNG vs A's 9KB), so B's selection field is not one colour — 204,237,248 / 203,237,248 / 204,236,248 mixed. Invisible at 1x but the band is technically not flat.
Neither implies blink or motion; nothing to judge on caret aliveness.
